title: Turning a provider's rate-limit response headers into quota buckets, in three languages
pins: Which quota buckets a given set of response headers produces, what each is NAMED, and what a reset MEANS. Quota is a fact about an account, not about a process: a PHP worker and a Python worker drawing on one key both read these headers to decide whether to send the next request, and a record of what the provider said is routinely written by one service and read by another. A disagreement here never errors. One language throttles on a bucket the other cannot see, or retries into a limit it believes has lifted, or stores an instant the other reads back as a different string. Two rows go further and ask whether a header can abort the parse of a successful, already-paid-for response -- a header being chosen by whatever proxy sits in front of the provider, not by the provider alone.
scope: Turning one provider's RESPONSE HEADERS into rate-limit buckets, for the three providers every port implements. NOT the request side, NOT retry or back-off policy, NOT the 429 error path -- a rate-limited request raises before any of this runs -- and NOT streaming, whose headers arrive on a response this parser never sees. A green run says the three languages read the same headers the same way; it says nothing about whether anything then acts on them, and today nothing in any of the three ports does.
construction: Each row hands one provider's headers to that provider's reader with the clock FROZEN, and records the buckets exactly as each language's own value object serialises them. Headers are handed over with their case intact, and every runner says so in a comment, because lower-casing in a runner would answer prl-0008 -- the title-casing proxy -- in the harness instead of in the package. Two of the three providers report a reset as a DURATION, so a frozen clock is what makes those rows a comparison rather than a measurement of elapsed time.
findings: TEN OF SIXTEEN ROWS DISAGREE, and no per-language suite could see any of them, because each language asserts against the value its own code produced. This value had never been compared across languages at all: G-15 recorded that prism-py had no ProviderRateLimit while prism-ts did, and the register predicted a one-sided gap. What the suite found instead is that the two REFERENCES disagree with each other, on nine rows, before Python is considered. (1) prl-0001, THE CONTROL, disagrees on ORDER alone: the reference walks the anthropic-ratelimit- prefix generically and reports buckets in header order, while prism-ts enumerates four names and reports them in its own. Same four buckets, different rate_limits[0]. (2) prl-0003: a bucket nobody enumerated (web search) is reported by the reference and INVISIBLE to prism-ts -- which is indistinguishable from a response that carried no quota at all. (3) prl-0014 is the worst: Mistral sends ratelimitbysize-limit with no bucket segment, which the reference reads and its own tests assert against, while prism-ts reads ratelimitbysize-limit-tokens and therefore returns NOTHING for a real Mistral response. (4) prl-0002: the reference parses a reset sent as a unix epoch -- a shape it has a named test for -- and prism-ts produces Invalid Date and drops the reset silently. (5) prl-0004: a bucket whose limit arrived without its remaining is reported by the reference with a null remaining and dropped entirely by prism-ts. (6) prl-0005: the reference preserves the wire offset (+02:00) and prism-ts normalises to UTC, so the same instant stores as different bytes depending on which language wrote the record. (7) prl-0006 is the security row: an unparseable reset makes the REFERENCE RAISE, so one mangled header aborts the parse of a completion the caller has already paid for. Both ports return no known reset and keep the response. (8) prl-0015: with no rate-limit headers at all the reference still emits a tokens bucket reading limit 0, remaining 0, resets now -- a provider that said nothing, reported as exhausted. (9) prl-0016: a prefixed header with no bucket segment becomes a bucket NAMED limit in the reference and in prism-py, and nothing in prism-ts. (10) prl-0008 is the one row where prism-py stands alone, and deliberately: HTTP field names are case-insensitive, both references compare their prefix case-sensitively, and a single title-casing proxy therefore makes both report no rate limits at all -- invisibly, since that is also what a response without the headers legitimately looks like. Where prism-py diverges from the reference it is on rows 6, 8 and 15 plus the UTC normalisation in row 5, each a case decision 0002 calls 'the reference is the one that is wrong': the port contract is the golden, not the defect. Everywhere else it follows the reference, including the generic prefix walk, the epoch reset, the partial bucket and the malformed bucket name. Six rows agree in all three languages, and one of those is not reassuring: prl-0012 records that the compound duration OpenAI really sends (1m30s) is matched by NONE of the three, because all three anchor the same pattern at both ends. That row exists because a corpus compares languages and is blind by construction to a bug they share -- the G-36 lesson, asked about a different field.
construction_note: Every column is EXECUTED, not transcribed. The reference half runs the shipped traits by composing them into three tiny classes -- three, and not one, because all three readers are named processRateLimits and PHP refuses the composition outright. That collision is worth stating rather than aliasing away: the reference has one name for three genuinely different readers, which is exactly how a port implements one of them and believes it has implemented rate limits.

discrimination.gap: No probe names this suite. That is true of every security-corpus in this repository -- the probe machinery in probes/probes.json drives the five golden-based kinds through the ports' conformance runners, and a security-corpus is deliberately not run from there, so a mutant has nothing to fail. The other nine security corpora nevertheless declare status 'probed', which no probe backs; this one says what is actually true rather than inheriting the claim. What would close it is a mutant that can be installed around a family repo's own corpus test.

php.note: The reference, and the source of the php column. Run with --check it fails when the shipped traits stop producing what is recorded. It is the generator rather than a test in prism itself because the readers are protected trait methods with no public surface; the generator composes the traits so the SHIPPED code runs, and rewriting the logic would measure the generator instead of the package.

ts.note: Recorded by prism-parity:tools/record-provider-rate-limits.mjs, which imports prism-ts's dist/ from the sibling checkout and freezes Date.now per row -- both duration readers call it directly rather than taking an injectable clock. The test in prism-ts then asserts the port still produces every recorded row, so the nine divergences above are PINNED: closing any of them is a deliberate act that has to update this corpus, not a quiet edit.

py.note: Recorded by prism-parity:tools/record_provider_rate_limits.py, which imports prism-py from the sibling checkout. This port had NO rate-limit reader at all until 2026-09-05 (G-15) and every provider reported an empty list; the suite was written as part of closing that, which is why its first run compares three implementations rather than confirming two.
